title: Detection Strategy for SVG Smuggling with Script Execution and Delivery Behavior
shortTitle: Detection Strategy for SVG Smuggling with Script Executio...
summary: This detection strategy covers SVG smuggling with script execution and delivery behaviour, a sub technique grouped under T1027.017 for obfuscated files. A scalable vector graphics file is a text and XML document that browsers and some document viewers render, and because it can legally contain script and external references it is an attractive container for code that static filters treat as an image. The telemetry that makes this visible is file creation events with the image extension, script host or browser child process creation, object identifier and macro events from office applications, and network records showing the file arriving from mail or web content. The usual failure mode is that SVG files are ordinary marketing and design assets, so the rule only stays useful when the script execution or the unusual delivery path is required rather than the file type alone.

beginner.definition: This rule looks for a picture file that also carries hidden instructions. The picture type is called scalable vector graphics, or SVG, and it is really a text document that describes shapes. Some tools that open it will also run any script inside it. The rule watches for that script running and for how the file arrived.
beginner.whyItMatters: Filters and users both treat a picture as harmless. So this file type slips past controls that block documents and programs. The file often arrives in an email attachment or a download and looks like a normal image. It also keeps the original code hidden inside text, which may be hard for a person to read. This makes the delivery step quiet and hard to notice.
howItWorks: The file monitoring agent records every new file, with its full name, folder and who created it.
The rule keeps files whose name ends with the picture extension for scalable vector graphics.
It excludes files written by signed design applications inside their own project folders.
The rule then looks for a script host starting as a child of the program that opened the file.
Network and mail records are joined to see whether the file arrived as an attachment or a download.
A file that arrived from outside plus a script child process is treated as one alert.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital sign in sheet. It looks like a plain form, but a stranger has written their own instructions in the margin. Staff read the form and follow the margin note, because it sits on a page they already trust. This rule checks both the form and the note in the margin.
takeaways: A file extension is a label, not a promise about what the file can do.
Alert on execution and delivery, not on every SVG file on the disk.
Open untrusted image files in a disposable environment, never on a working laptop.

objectives: Explain why an SVG file can contain script even though users treat it as an image.
Identify file creation events that record the full path, extension and creating process.
Recognise a script host or browser process starting as a child of a document or image viewer.
Trace the delivery channel of a suspicious file using browser and mail records.
Apply allow list filters for design software and asset management tools.
Describe a safe handling step for a suspicious attachment before anyone opens it.
dataSources: Sysmon event 11 file creation including TargetFilename, Image and the creating user
Sysmon event 1 process creation showing a script host as a child of a document viewer
Sysmon event 7 image load of a scripting engine library inside a viewer process
Mail gateway attachment records listing file name, content type and sender for inbound messages
Proxy web download records showing the content type and referrer for a fetched file
logic: The pattern is a file with a scalable vector graphics extension that is written to a user writable location shortly after arriving through mail or web download, combined with a script host starting as a child of the application that opened the file. The fields that must be correlated are the file name and directory on the creation event, the parent and child image on the process creation event, and the sender or download source on the delivery records, joined on host and user within a short window. The malicious case usually shows the file written outside a managed asset repository, an office or viewer process spawning a script interpreter, and a delivery source that does not belong to a known content partner. The benign case is the design team saving assets from a signed creative suite whose install path is fixed, where no script interpreter is ever created.
pseudoQuery:
# title: SVG File Written from a Download Location Followed by Script Host
# logsource:
#   product: windows
# detection:
#   selection_file:
#     EventID: 11
#     TargetFilename|endswith: '.svg'
#   selection_exec:
#     EventID: 1
#     ParentImage|endswith:
#       - '\WINWORD.EXE'
#       - '\outlook.exe'
#   filter_design:
#     Image|endswith:
#       - '\Illustrator.exe'
#       - '\Inkscape.exe'
#   condition: (selection_file or selection_exec) and not filter_design
# level: medium
falsePositives: Design and marketing teams saving real vector assets that are opened later by a viewer with scripting support
Catalogues and product feed importers that convert vendor supplied vector files as a batch job
Document management systems that preview vector attachments and launch a converter process as a result
Web applications that generate vector charts on the fly and store them in a temporary directory
Software packaging pipelines that include vector icons in an installer and touch them during a build
tuningNotes: Scope the rule to user workstations and exclude known asset repositories, content management shares and build servers, because those produce the bulk of legitimate vector files. Require either a script interpreter child process or a delivery source outside your content partners before raising an alert, and treat the file event alone as low priority enrichment. Baseline how many vector files your design tools create per day and from which paths. The coverage you lose is a malicious vector file that is written directly by a signed design tool, and one that is opened by an application that runs its script code in process without starting a visible child.
